result.name: John F. Kennedy International Airport
result.period: calendar year 2025 (BTS T-100 and On-Time data); growth compares 2025 with 2024. Not a live or trailing-12-month figure.
result.note: A null metric was suppressed in the source data (too few flights); say so, never guess it. Quote these figures exactly; never answer an airport figure from memory.
result.facts_summary: JFK, calendar year 2025: 31,021,616 enplaned passengers; 17,009,706 of them international (54.8%); passengers down 1.4% from 2024 (31,464,221 in 2024); average departure delay 17.47 minutes; 21.1% of departures 15 minutes or more late; cancellation rate 2%.

assumptions: Congestion is proxied by operational strain: average departure delay, the share of departures 15 minutes or more late, and the cancellation rate (BTS On-Time Reporting Carrier data, calendar year 2025). Seat load factor is scored separately in the unmet-demand and expansion scores.

Metrics are compared as rates (per flight), not totals, so large hubs and small airports are judged on the same footing. Each input is scaled 0-1 between anchors set by one rule: the 5th and 95th percentile of that input across the dataset's airports, rounded to two significant figures.
congestion.uncertainty: Delays are 2025 averages for the large reporting carriers (and their regional partners) on domestic flights. Short-term peaks are smoothed out, weather is mixed with true capacity saturation, and a smaller airport's delays often originate at the hubs its flights go to. Rates are never defaulted: an airport with under 5,000 scheduled departures in the BTS On-Time data, or under 365 departures in T-100, has that rate suppressed and the score is shown as insufficient data.

assumptions: 'Unmet demand' has no direct public measurement (bookings that never happened aren't observable in free data). We estimate it as a composite lower-bound proxy.
Load factor (passengers / seats on departing scheduled flights, BTS T-100 2025, all carriers) is the primary signal: sustained high seat utilization implies demand that current supply cannot absorb.
Passenger growth (2025 vs 2024) measured against how hard the runways are already worked indicates a widening gap; a declining airport scores below a flat one.
unmet_demand.uncertainty: This is a lower-bound proxy. True unmet demand (searches that didn't convert, fares that priced people out) requires proprietary GDS/OAG data not available for free. Rates are never defaulted: an airport with under 5,000 scheduled departures in the BTS On-Time data, or under 365 departures in T-100, has that rate suppressed and the score is shown as insufficient data.

assumptions: Investment thesis (demand-side): the case for terminal expansion is strongest where strong, growing demand meets a capacity-constrained airport — so renovation unlocks revenue rather than adding idle space.

Score blends passenger growth (2025 vs 2024), current congestion, seat load pressure, and passenger volume (every enplaned passenger, domestic and international, all carriers); weights are documented and adjustable. Each input is scaled 0-1 between anchors set by one rule: the 5th and 95th percentile of that input across the dataset's airports, rounded to two significant figures.
Airport scope is limited to the bundled dataset: the 100 busiest U.S. airports by 2025 passengers, plus Burlington (BTV) and Manchester (MHT).
expansion.uncertainty: Score reflects demand-side opportunity only. It does not model construction cost, land/gate availability, or local regulatory limits (e.g. noise curfews), which a full investment case would weigh. Growth is a single year (2025 vs 2024).

assumptions: Investment thesis (demand-side): the case for terminal expansion is strongest where strong, growing demand meets a capacity-constrained airport — so renovation unlocks revenue rather than adding idle space.
